extracted.intended_audience: software inventors, patent applicants, and patent practitioners considering Beauregard claims
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on whether and how to use Beauregard claims (computer-program-as-product claims) in patent applications, including claim form, benefits, risks, and eligibility considerations. Aimed at helping inventors and attorneys weigh pros/cons for software-related inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauregard claim definition / claim form
rubrics_metrics.description: A Beauregard claim is a type of claim in a patent application that claims a computer program as a product, rather than a process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically written as a claim to an article of manufacture (e.g., a computer-readable medium on which instructions are encoded for carrying out a process). May include a preamble describing the general nature of the invention. Can be used for programs stored on tangible media (floppy disks, CD-ROMs) and, in some cases, for programs stored on intangible media (the internet).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent eligibility risk under 35 U.S.C. §101 and Alice
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauregard claims may be at risk of invalidation under §101, especially after Alice, which held that a claim merely reciting an abstract idea is not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea and whether it includes a sufficient inventive concept. The Supreme Court's skepticism about software patentability (Alice) means Beauregard claims require careful drafting to survive eligibility challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broader protection (advantage)
rubrics_metrics.description: By focusing on the overall functionality, Beauregard claims can provide broader protection than claims that focus solely on individual hardware components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broader protection can make it harder for infringers to avoid liability by making minor modifications to products. Use Beauregard claims when broader coverage of software functionality is strategically important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and precision (advantage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauregard claims can often be more precise and easier to understand than claims that solely focus on hardware components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear, precise claim language can make it easier to determine whether a product infringes. Draft claims to clearly define the encoded instructions and their functionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility (advantage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauregard claims can be adapted to cover a wide range of inventions, from simple software applications to complex hardware systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They are versatile and can be tailored to different types of software-related inventions, but drafting should reflect the intended scope and implementation details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enhanced enforcement (advantage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauregard claims can be easier to enforce in court, as they can more clearly define the scope of the invention and make it easier to prove infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear product-oriented claim language (e.g., medium with encoded instructions) may simplify infringement analyses compared to certain process claims, but enforcement still depends on proving the claim elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited scope (disadvantage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauregard claims are often limited in scope because they focus on specific steps or processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such focus can make it difficult to protect broader concepts or inventions; consider complementing Beauregard claims with other claim types if broader coverage is desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complexity of drafting and understanding (disadvantage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauregard claims can be complex to draft and understand, especially for those not familiar with patent law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complexity can increase the cost and time required to obtain a patent. Ensure skilled counsel drafts the claims to balance clarity, scope, and eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent eligibility challenges specifically under the Alice test (disadvantage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauregard claims may face patent eligibility challenges, particularly under the Alice test which requires claims be directed to patent-eligible subject matter and have sufficient inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting, emphasize how the claim is more than an abstract idea (e.g., tie to technological improvements or concrete implementation details) to reduce Alice risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty in enforcement due to proving steps/sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Enforcing Beauregard claims can be challenging because it may require proving that the infringer has performed all of the claimed steps in the exact sequence specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how infringement will be proven in practice; if proof of exact step sequence is difficult, weigh alternative claim strategies or drafting approaches that avoid rigid step sequencing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of claim narrowing during prosecution or litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: If a Beauregard claim is overly broad, it may be narrowed during prosecution or in litigation, which can limit its effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft with care to avoid overbroad language that invites narrowing; consider fallback claim sets and claim amendments that preserve value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of storage medium (tangible vs intangible)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauregard claims have historically been used for programs stored on tangible media but can also be used for programs stored on intangible media like the internet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The choice of medium affects claim drafting and potential eligibility/enforcement issues; be explicit about the medium when beneficial, but recognize that claiming intangible distribution/storage may raise additional challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical precedent and examples as guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauregard claims were recognized following In re Beauregard (1995) and have been used in notable patents (examples: Amazon one-click, Microsoft Windows, Apple iPod patents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precedent examples to inform strategy but account for evolving case law (e.g., Alice). Past grants do not guarantee current validity—assess current jurisprudence when deciding to file.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation to consult experienced patent attorney
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are considering filing a patent application for a computer program, you should consult with an experienced patent attorney to discuss whether a Beauregard claim is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An attorney can help weigh benefits and drawbacks, advise on drafting to mitigate eligibility and enforcement risks, and recommend complementary claim types or prosecution strategies.
